custom-chin-implant-silicone-medpor.summary: A shaped silicone or porous implant placed over the chin bone to add projection, height or width, giving a stronger profile that is visible once healed.

quick.overview:
A chin implant is a shaped piece of silicone or porous polyethylene (Medpor) placed over the chin bone to push a recessed chin forward. It gives a stronger, more balanced side profile, and can also add height or width.

The implant sits on the front of the jawbone and adds bulk through a cut under the chin or inside the lower lip. Silicone is smooth and removable; porous polyethylene allows tissue ingrowth. Custom implants are designed from a CT scan of the individual's jaw. It is a long-established cosmetic operation, often done alongside nose surgery, and outcomes are documented mainly in surgical case series.
quick.how: People usually see a surgeon for a consultation and imaging, then have a short operation under anaesthetic. It is often chosen as a less invasive alternative to a sliding genioplasty, and is frequently combined with rhinoplasty. Swelling settles over weeks and the final profile is visible once healed. Forum users compare stock implants with custom designs and discuss whether an implant is enough for a very recessed chin.
quick.risks: Reported risks include swelling, hematoma, infection, implant displacement, bone changes under the implant and nerve numbness. Complication rates depend on technique and surgeon experience. Implants can shift or be removed later, and porous polyethylene is harder to remove than silicone. It is an Rx surgical procedure performed by licensed surgeons.

angle.text: A chin implant adds projection, and sometimes height or width, to a recessed chin by placing material over the chin bone. The stronger, more balanced profile is visible once healed. Silicone, porous polyethylene and patient-specific designs are used, with outcomes documented in surgical case series.

chin-filler.summary: Injectable filler, usually hyaluronic acid, placed at the chin to add projection or length without surgery; the profile change shows right away and is temporary.

quick.overview:
Chin filler, sometimes called a liquid genioplasty, adds projection or length to the chin without surgery. The change in profile is visible right after treatment, and people use it to get a fuller, more defined chin or to preview a surgical result.

A clinician injects a gel, most often hyaluronic acid, near the bone to add volume. Companies have registered trials of several products for chin retrusion, and a published case review of 83 patients describes combined forehead, nose and chin filler used to alter the profile. The effect lasts as long as the material persists, and hyaluronic acid can be dissolved with hyaluronidase.
quick.how: Treatment is a short clinic visit with no surgery and little downtime. People use it as a temporary alternative to implants and genioplasty, or as a trial run before committing to surgery. Results fade as the body gradually absorbs the gel, so many repeat treatments to maintain the look.
quick.risks: The chin is generally regarded as a lower-risk injection area, but case reports describe vascular occlusion, skin necrosis and tongue necrosis after chin filler. Anatomical studies map the arteries to guide safer injection. Fillers are regulated medical devices given by licensed practitioners, and clinicians regard self-injection posted on forums as outside safe conditions.

angle.text: Chin filler adds projection or length to the chin with an injected gel, so the profile looks fuller and more defined right after treatment. People use it to preview or approximate surgical results. Hyaluronic acid fillers have been studied for chin augmentation, and the effect is temporary.

vertical-chin-lengthening.summary: Genioplasty, graft or implant surgery that makes the chin taller rather than just more forward, giving a longer, better-balanced lower face once healed.

quick.overview:
Vertical chin lengthening is a set of surgical methods that increase the height of the chin. It is used by people with a short lower third of the face who want a taller chin rather than a more forward one, for a longer, better-balanced lower face.

In an osseous genioplasty the chin segment is cut, moved down and held in place, with a bone graft or other material filling the gap. Implants can also add height, and some variants combine lengthening with narrowing. Surgeons describe it for short lower faces, including in East Asian contouring surgery. The published literature is mostly technique papers and small case series.
quick.how: Patients plan the operation with a surgeon using imaging, and it is done under anaesthetic, sometimes together with other jaw or chin work. The height change is visible once swelling settles, over weeks to months. Graft-based and implant-based routes are the main options discussed.
quick.risks: The literature mentions infection, donor-site problems and resorption of grafted bone as drawbacks of graft-based methods. It is a surgical procedure performed by licensed surgeons, with the usual anaesthetic and recovery considerations.

angle.text: Vertical chin lengthening makes a short chin taller by moving the chin bone down and filling the gap with a graft or by adding an implant, giving a longer, more balanced lower face. The height change is visible once healed. The surgical literature consists mostly of small case series.

chin-reduction-shaving.summary: Surgery that shrinks a long, protruding or wide chin by burring the bone or moving it back, giving a smaller, more proportionate lower face.

quick.overview:
Chin reduction is surgery to make a long, protruding or wide chin smaller. The aim is a more proportionate lower face, and the reduction is visible once healed.

The two classical approaches are an osteotomy that cuts the chin bone and moves it back or up (reduction or setback genioplasty), and burring the surface of the bone down. Another described approach removes bone and soft tissue from under the chin. It also appears alongside mandibular setback for a long chin and in feminization surgery. The published literature is technique descriptions and case series.
quick.how: Patients plan with a surgeon, who chooses between repositioning the bone and shaving it based on the shape of the chin. It is done under anaesthetic, and swelling settles over weeks to months before the final contour shows.
quick.risks: Surgical papers state that both main approaches have potential negative aesthetic sequelae, including mental nerve injury, bony contour irregularities, increased submental soft-tissue fullness and chin pad ptosis. It is performed under anaesthetic by licensed surgeons.

angle.text: Chin reduction shrinks a chin that looks too large or prominent by burring the bone or cutting and moving it back, for a smaller, better-proportioned lower face. The change is visible once healed. Techniques are described in surgical papers and case series.

double-jaw-surgery-for-retrognathia.summary: Bimaxillary surgery that moves a recessed lower jaw forward along with the upper jaw, giving a stronger jawline, profile and bite once healed.

quick.overview:
Double-jaw (bimaxillary) surgery repositions both the upper and lower jaw to correct a recessed lower jaw (retrognathia), bite problems and facial proportions. It is the major structural option for a stronger jawline and profile, and the skeletal change is visible and measurable after healing.

Surgeons typically cut the lower jaw with a bilateral sagittal split osteotomy and the upper jaw with a Le Fort I osteotomy, move them to a planned position and fix them with plates and screws. Planning uses imaging and often 3D software, and it is done together with an orthodontist. It is a long-established operation in oral and maxillofacial surgery, sometimes combined with a genioplasty.
quick.how: Treatment usually starts with braces to prepare the teeth, then surgery under general anaesthetic, then more orthodontic finishing. Recovery is typically measured in weeks to months. Forum users discuss it at the top of the hardmaxxing ladder and compare it with single-jaw surgery plus genioplasty.
quick.risks: Reported risks include temporary or permanent numbness from nerve injury, infection, bleeding and swelling, and in some patients condylar atrophy or joint changes. It is major surgery performed by oral and maxillofacial surgeons.

angle.text: Double-jaw surgery moves the lower jaw forward and repositions the upper jaw to match, improving both bite and side profile for a stronger jawline. The skeletal change is visible and measurable after healing. It is a well-established orthognathic operation with an extensive surgical literature.

profile-analysis-ricketts-e-line.summary: A line from nose tip to chin used on side-profile photos to judge where the lips sit, helping you see chin and lip balance.

quick.overview:
The Ricketts esthetic line, or E-line, is drawn from the tip of the soft-tissue nose to the soft-tissue chin (pogonion) on a side-view image. Measuring where the lips sit against it gives you a concrete read on how full or retrusive your profile is.

Orthodontists use the lower-lip distance to the E-line as a standard measurement, and orthodontic and surgical planning use it. A published mean for lower lip to E-line is minus 2 mm with a standard deviation of 2 mm. Studies also show that preferred lip positions differ among observer groups.
quick.how: People take a straight side-on photo or use a lateral cephalogram, draw the line and see how far the lips fall from it. They use the result to decide whether chin or lip changes are of interest, and discuss it alongside other profile analyses.
quick.risks: This is a measurement convention, not a treatment, so it carries no physical risk. Cephalometric measurements are two-dimensional, norms are population averages, and preferred profiles differ among observers of different backgrounds.

angle.text: Forum users draw the E-line on side-profile photos to see where the lips sit relative to the nose and chin, then decide whether chin or lip changes are of interest. It is a standard orthodontic reference measurement. Preferred lip positions vary between observers and over time.

orthodontic-functional-appliances-herbst.summary: Orthodontist-fitted jaw-advancing appliances for growing teens with an overbite, used to bring a recessed lower jaw forward for a better-balanced profile and bite.

quick.overview:
Functional appliances such as the Herbst and Twin Block hold the lower jaw forward in children and teens with a Class II bite, where the lower jaw sits behind the upper. The payoff is a better-balanced profile and bite while the face is still growing.

The Herbst uses telescoping rods fixed to the teeth; the Twin Block uses removable interlocking bite plates. The Twin Block was studied in a multicentre randomized trial in the United Kingdom in children aged 8 to 10. Research, including a systematic review, separates small amounts of extra lower-jaw growth and upper-jaw restraint from movement of the teeth themselves.
quick.how: An orthodontist fits the appliance, usually before or around the pubertal growth spurt. The Herbst is fixed, so it does not depend on remembering to wear it, and treatment typically runs for several months. The Twin Block is removable and worn as directed. Forum users ask about cost, adult use and cheaper substitutes.
quick.risks: Reported effects include initial discomfort, chewing and speech difficulty, spacing between teeth, and possible gum or root effects with heavy tooth movement. The appliances are designed for growing patients, and skeletal change in adults is limited without surgery. Over-the-counter substitutes have not been studied for this purpose.

angle.text: Herbst and Twin Block appliances hold the lower jaw forward in growing teens, so the jaw grows or shifts forward and the profile and bite balance out. Randomized trials in adolescents have studied them, with debate over how much change is jaw growth versus tooth movement. Adult use for facial appearance is based on user reports.

neck-posture-forward-head-correction.summary: Pulling the head back over the shoulders so the chin, neck and jawline line up better in profile; well studied for neck pain, not yet for facial appearance.

quick.overview:
Forward head posture is when the head sits ahead of the shoulders, so the chin appears to poke forward. People work on correcting it to line the chin and neck up better and show a sharper jawline and profile when upright.

It is common with heavy screen use and is usually measured with the craniovertebral angle. Most research on it concerns neck pain, headache and disability, and a 2019 meta-analysis found a correlation with neck pain in adults but not in adolescents. Forum posters disagree on the look: some say correction improves the profile, others say a chin tuck can make a recessed chin look less prominent. No published study has tested its effect on facial appearance.
quick.how: Correction usually means postural habits, ergonomic changes (screen height, seating) and neck and upper-back strengthening and stretching exercises. People check progress with side-view photos taken from the same distance.
quick.risks: Posture exercises are generally low risk and are studied mainly in the context of neck pain. Some forum users report that a strong chin tuck makes a recessed chin look less prominent, so results in photos can vary by person.

angle.text: Pulling the head back over the shoulders lines the chin and neck up better, which proponents say sharpens the jawline and profile. Posture correction is well studied for neck pain; its effect on how the chin and jaw look has not been tested. Forum users disagree on whether it helps or hurts a recessed chin.

jaw-advancement-for-sleep-apnea-mad-devi.summary: A night-time mouthpiece that holds the lower jaw forward to open the airway; some people wonder if it also helps jaw position and profile.

quick.overview:
Mandibular advancement devices (MADs) are mouthpieces worn during sleep that hold the lower jaw slightly forward to keep the airway open. They are prescribed for snoring and obstructive sleep apnea, and some forum users wonder whether the forward jaw position could also improve their profile.

They are medical products rather than facial-aesthetics tools. Guidelines from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the American Academy of Dental Sleep Medicine recommend oral appliances for primary snoring and for people with sleep apnea who cannot tolerate CPAP, and randomized trials have compared MADs with CPAP. No published trial has tested them for changing facial appearance.
quick.how: A dentist or sleep specialist fits the device after assessment, and it is worn each night. The effect on the airway lasts only while the device is in. It is often used when CPAP is not tolerated.
quick.risks: Reported effects include dry mouth, tooth and jaw pain, and long-term changes in how the teeth meet. Many users stop because of discomfort. Cheap non-prescription versions have not been studied, and some specialists consider them potentially dangerous.

angle.text: Some forum users wonder whether wearing a sleep-apnea mouthpiece that holds the lower jaw forward could shift the jaw for a better profile. These devices are well studied for snoring and breathing during sleep, while any effect on facial appearance has not been tested.

fat-grafting-to-chin.summary: Your own fat, harvested and injected to build out a small chin, giving a fuller, more defined chin as a surgical alternative to implants or fillers.

quick.overview:
Fat grafting moves your own fat from elsewhere on the body into the chin to add volume and projection. The result is a fuller, more defined chin, visible after treatment, using natural tissue instead of an implant or filler.

Fat is harvested, processed and reinjected. Part of it survives as living tissue and part is reabsorbed; transferred fat behaves like fat elsewhere in the body, so weight gain or loss can affect results. Fat grafting is an established technique in general, with up to 50% resorption cited for breast augmentation, and the sources reviewed give no outcome data specific to the chin.
quick.how: It is a surgical procedure: fat is taken by liposuction, prepared and injected into the chin area. It is discussed as an alternative to implants, sliding genioplasty and injectable fillers, and sometimes done in more than one session as the fat settles.
quick.risks: Reported general risks include fat necrosis, swelling, bruising, asymmetry or lumpiness, infection and donor-site pain. Some grafted fat can be reabsorbed, so volume may change. It is performed by clinicians.

angle.text: Fat grafting builds out a small chin with your own fat, as an alternative to implants, genioplasty or fillers, and the added volume is visible after treatment. It is an established technique in general, with limited chin-specific data, and some of the fat can be reabsorbed.

weight-loss-for-chin-definition.summary: Losing body fat to reduce fullness under the chin so the chin and jawline show more clearly, most useful where a double chin is soft tissue.

quick.overview:
Lowering overall body fat reduces fullness under the chin, so the chin and jawline look sharper. It works on the covering fat, not on bone structure.

A double chin can come from subcutaneous fat around the neck creating a fold, or from jaw bones that do not project far enough forward, often in people of normal weight. Where the cause is fat, losing fat shrinks the fat cells under the chin along with the rest of the body. No study has tested weight loss specifically for chin appearance, and the sources reviewed do not address whether fat can be lost from the chin area selectively.
quick.how: People reduce body fat through diet and training over weeks to months and watch the jawline and under-chin area in side-view photos. Surgical fat removal and jaw or chin surgery are described for those whose double chin is fat or bony.
quick.risks: No risks specific to this approach are described in the sources reviewed. When the cause is bone structure, fat loss does not change the chin's projection.

angle.text: Lowering body fat reduces fullness under the chin, so the chin and jawline show more clearly, mainly where a double chin is soft tissue. It changes the covering fat rather than bone structure. No studies test fat loss specifically for chin definition.

submalar-filler.summary: Filler injected below the cheekbone to add lower-midface volume for a fuller, lifted cheek contour; visible after treatment and temporary.

quick.overview:
Submalar filler adds volume to the hollow beneath the cheekbones, giving a fuller or more defined lower midface and a lifted cheek contour. The change is visible after treatment.

It is a non-surgical counterpart to submalar implants, which augment the midface while malar implants sit on the cheekbones. A clinician injects a gel filler, typically hyaluronic acid, into the tissue below the cheekbone, adding volume until the body gradually resorbs it. Small registered trials have tested hyaluronic acid and other fillers for midface volume and cheek augmentation.
quick.how: It is a short clinic treatment with little downtime. People choose it as a temporary, reversible way to try a fuller cheek contour, and repeat it as the filler is absorbed.
quick.risks: Asymmetry from uneven resorption or shifting is listed among the risks of cheek augmentation. Filler is eventually resorbed, so results are temporary. Fillers are given by licensed practitioners.

angle.text: Submalar filler adds volume in the hollow beneath the cheekbone for a fuller, lifted cheek contour, as a non-surgical counterpart to submalar implants. The change is visible after treatment and is temporary. Small registered trials have tested fillers for midface volume.

malar-augmentation-with-fat-grafting.summary: Your own liposuctioned fat injected into the cheeks to add volume and projection over the cheekbones for fuller, higher-looking cheeks.

quick.overview:
Malar fat grafting uses your own fat, taken from elsewhere on the body, processed and injected into the cheeks. It adds fullness and projection over the cheekbones for a fuller, higher-looking cheek, and the added volume is visible after treatment.

It is a form of autologous soft-tissue augmentation, distinct from cheek implants and hyaluronic acid fillers, and is discussed as a natural-tissue alternative to both. Fat is harvested by liposuction, purified and reinjected; the portion that survives provides lasting volume and the rest is resorbed. Fat grafting is widely used in the face, and general sources describe it restoring volume to deflated facial compartments. Cheek-specific evidence is limited in the sources reviewed.
quick.how: It is a surgical procedure in two steps, harvesting and injection, often under local or general anaesthetic. Results settle as swelling goes down and the grafted fat establishes, and some people have follow-up sessions.
quick.risks: Reported risks include swelling, bruising, infection, lumpiness or contour irregularity, fat necrosis and unpredictable resorption, so outcomes can vary. It is a medical procedure performed by surgeons.

angle.text: Fat grafting adds volume and projection over the cheekbones using your own tissue, as an alternative to implants or hyaluronic acid fillers, for fuller, higher-looking cheeks. The added fullness is visible after treatment. It is widely used in the face, with limited cheek-specific data and some reabsorption.

zygomatic-arch-reduction-reduction-malar.summary: Cheekbone-narrowing surgery that cuts and repositions the zygoma, giving a slimmer, softer face shape once healed; commonly requested in East Asia.

quick.overview:
Reduction malarplasty cuts and repositions the cheekbone (zygoma) or zygomatic arch to narrow a wide or prominent midface. The result is a slimmer, softer face shape, visible after healing. Surgeons describe it as one of the more commonly requested facial-contour procedures in East Asia.

Osteotomies are made in the malar complex or zygomatic arch and the bone is repositioned and fixed. Techniques have moved from coronal-incision approaches, which leave a scalp scar and carry facial-nerve risk, toward intraoral and limited-incision methods. The literature is mostly surgeon case series and technique papers. In looksmaxxing forums the related ZSO term mostly appears in discussions about the opposite aim, projecting cheekbones.
quick.how: It is planned with imaging and done under general anaesthetic through coronal, intraoral, preauricular or small percutaneous incisions. Swelling and bone healing take weeks to months before the final shape shows.
quick.risks: Reported concerns include scars and facial-nerve injury with some approaches, and zygomatic nonunion after surgery. It is major bone surgery performed by trained surgeons.

angle.text: Reduction malarplasty narrows wide or prominent cheekbones by cutting and repositioning the bone, giving a slimmer, softer face shape visible after healing. It is among the more commonly requested facial-contour procedures in East Asia, described mainly in surgeon case series.

cheekbone-makeup-contour-highlight.summary: Shading beneath the cheekbone and highlighting on top to make cheekbones look higher and sharper instantly; washes off and carries little risk.

quick.overview:
Cheekbone contouring uses darker shades beneath the cheekbone and lighter or shimmering shades on top to make cheekbones look more defined, higher and sharper. The effect is visible immediately, for photos or an evening.

Shading and highlighting change the perceived depth and shape of the cheek through light and shadow. It is a cosmetic styling technique rather than a medical treatment, and no clinical studies of the effect were found. It is discussed in the style-focused parts of appearance communities as a non-surgical, reversible way to change perceived facial structure.
quick.how: People apply a contour shade in the hollow under the cheekbone and blend it out, then place highlighter on the top of the bone. Results depend on lighting and application, and the look washes off at the end of the day.
quick.risks: Makeup carries the usual risks of skin irritation or allergic reaction with some products. The effect is temporary and washes off.

angle.text: Darker shades beneath the cheekbone and lighter or shimmering shades on top shift light and shadow so cheekbones look higher and more defined. The effect is visible immediately and washes off. It is a cosmetic technique, not a medical treatment.

midface-lift.summary: Surgery that lifts sagging cheek and lower-eyelid tissue to restore a fuller, younger-looking midface once healed.

quick.overview:
A midface lift raises sagging cheek and lower-eyelid tissue to restore volume, reduce a hollowed lower lid and give a fuller, younger-looking cheek. The lift is visible once healed. It is typically described as suited to people in their 40s without marked jowling.

Surgeons elevate and resuspend midface soft tissue using approaches such as the malar fat pad or high SMAS flap, through incisions near the hairline, eyelid or mouth. Techniques have changed over decades, and published evidence consists mainly of surgeon case series and technique reviews. It is frequently combined with eyelid surgery, and patients share combined facial-implant and rhinoplasty results in appearance communities.
quick.how: It is planned with a facial plastic surgeon and done under anaesthetic, often alongside eyelid surgery or other facial procedures. Swelling takes weeks to settle before the final result shows.
quick.risks: Reported complications in related eyelid and facelift surgery include lid malposition and dry-eye symptoms. It is major surgery performed by trained surgeons.

angle.text: A midface lift repositions sagging cheek and lower-eyelid tissue upward to restore a fuller, younger cheek and soften a hollowed lower lid. The lift is visible once healed. It is described as suited to people in their 40s without marked jowling, with evidence mostly from surgeon case series.

maxilla-expansion-for-forward-growth-fac.summary: An orthodontic facemask that pulls a growing child's upper jaw forward to improve midface support and profile; studied in children with underbites.

quick.overview:
Reverse-pull headgear, also called a facemask or face pulling device, is an orthodontic appliance used to bring the upper jaw and midface forward for better midface support and profile. It is used in children with underbites and a recessed upper jaw.

A frame rests on the forehead and chin, with elastics attached to the teeth to pull the upper jaw forward, often after rapid palatal expansion. Orthodontic literature reports that treatment in the deciduous and mixed dentition can produce forward skeletal movement of the maxilla through remodeling of the sutures around it, often with dentoalveolar effects. Forum users discuss it as a midface tool, though the evidence concerns growing children.
quick.how: An orthodontist fits the appliance and sets the elastics, and it is worn for set hours over months, typically in childhood when the sutures are still responsive. It is commonly paired with palatal expansion.
quick.risks: Dentoalveolar side effects are reported, and long-term follow-up shows some patients relapse. Use is guided by an orthodontist, and the evidence applies to growing children, not adults.

angle.text: Forum users discuss reverse-pull headgear, or face pulling, as a way to bring the upper jaw and midface forward for better support and profile. It has been studied in children with underbites and a recessed upper jaw; use as an adult appearance tool is based on user reports.

facial-thread-lift-cheek-lifting.summary: Threads placed under the skin to hoist the cheeks and soften the nasolabial fold without cutting skin away; minimally invasive with a visible lift afterward.

quick.overview:
A thread lift places threads, some with barbs or cones, under the skin to lift the cheeks and midface and soften the nasolabial fold, without removing skin. The lift is visible after the procedure.

The threads anchor and elevate tissue and are placed through small entry points. Wikipedia describes it as a simplified alternative to a facelift. Two trials are registered, one comparing hyaluronic acid-coated and non-coated threads for the midface and one combining threads with microfocused ultrasound; results were not available in the sources reviewed.
quick.how: It is a short, minimally invasive procedure done in a clinic, with less downtime than surgery. People choose it for a quick midface lift and softer fold lines instead of a facelift.
quick.risks: Physician and media reports describe infection, vessel puncture and pain, and some threads cannot easily be removed. Practitioner training and qualifications vary by country, and complications have drawn media scrutiny.

angle.text: Thread lifts raise the midface and soften the nasolabial fold by hoisting cheek tissue with threads placed under the skin, without removing skin. The lift is visible after the procedure. Efficacy data are limited and mixed, and complications are reported in the literature.

cheek-fat-pad-bichat-removal.summary: Surgery that removes part of the buccal fat pad to slim the lower cheek, giving hollower cheeks and a clearer cheekbone-to-jaw line once healed.

quick.overview:
Cheek fat pad (Bichat) removal, also called buccal fat removal or bichectomy, takes out part of the buccal fat pad, a mass of fat deep in the cheek, usually through an incision inside the mouth. The slimmer lower cheek is visible after healing, with hollower cheeks and a clearer cheekbone-to-jaw transition that users link to the ogee curve.

The pad sits between the buccinator muscle and the more superficial masseter and zygomaticus muscles, and it contributes to cheek fullness. Removing some of its volume reduces fullness in the lower cheek, which proponents say reveals cheekbone and jaw structure. The pad is well documented as a surgical flap in mouth and sinus surgery; published outcome data for purely cosmetic removal are limited.
quick.how: It is a short procedure through the inside of the mouth, usually under local anaesthetic or sedation, with swelling that settles over weeks. It is popular in looksmaxxing communities as a route to hollow cheeks, often considered alongside leanness.
quick.risks: Wikipedia reports a significant risk of injury to the buccal branch of the facial nerve and the parotid duct. Self-performed removal has been described on forums, and other members in those threads warn against it.

angle.text: Buccal fat removal is popular in looksmaxxing communities as a route to hollow cheeks and a more visible cheekbone-to-jaw transition, often tied to the ogee curve. Taking out part of the cheek fat pad slims the lower cheek once healed. Published outcome data for cosmetic removal are limited.

hollow-cheeks-via-chewing-then-fat-loss.summary: Build the masseter by chewing, then lean out to bring out cheekbones and jaw structure and create hollow cheeks.

quick.overview:
This approach pairs masseter-focused chewing with body and facial fat loss to bring out the cheekbones and the hollow below them. The goal is hollow cheeks with a more visible cheekbone and jaw.

Proponents describe the hollow as coming from cheekbone projection, jaw angle and masseter size, which become visible when facial fat is low. Wikipedia notes the buccal fat pad also contributes to cheek fullness. No clinical study of the combination was found, and forum members disagree about the look itself.
quick.how: People chew firm gum or tough foods to work the masseter while reducing body fat through diet and training over weeks to months, and track the cheeks and jaw in photos taken in consistent lighting.
quick.risks: No harms were documented for the combination in the sources reviewed. Medical literature associates very hollow cheeks with aging or lipodystrophy, conditions treated with volume restoration.

angle.text: Forum posters build the masseter with chewing and lower body and facial fat so cheekbones and jaw structure show more, creating hollow cheeks. They describe the hollow as coming from bone and muscle, revealed by less soft tissue. No studies test the combination.
